Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has replaced non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) as the preferred nomenclature for hepatic steatosis occurring in the context of cardiometabolic risk, a terminology shift intended to anchor diagnosis to positive metabolic criteria — obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, or dyslipidemia — rather than to the exclusion of alcohol use [@Mahoon2026Therapeutic]. The change is more than semantic: it is a recognition that MASLD is now the leading cause of chronic liver disease worldwide, affecting more than one-third of adults globally [@Tsai2026Metabolic; @Amorim2026GLP], and that its burden is inseparable from the parallel epidemics of obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), which nearly tripled global obesity prevalence since 1975 [@Henney2026The]. Within this spectrum, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) — the progressive, inflammatory and fibrogenic form of MASLD, historically termed non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) — represents the subset of patients at meaningful risk of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and liver-related mortality [@Li2026Liver; @Chan2026Pharmacological]. A related but distinct entity, metabolic and alcohol-associated liver disease (MetALD), describes the overlap phenotype in which cardiometabolic risk factors coexist with concurrent alcohol exposure, producing synergistic liver injury; because most MASLD trials exclude patients with significant alcohol use, MetALD-specific evidence remains sparse and is largely extrapolated from MASLD and alcohol-associated liver disease data [@Pagadala2026Pharmacologic].

Not all MASH carries equivalent prognostic weight, and the field has converged on the concept of "at-risk MASH" — steatohepatitis with fibrosis stage ≥2 — as the threshold that identifies patients most likely to benefit from pharmacotherapy and most likely to progress to cirrhosis if untreated [@Li2026Simplified]. Distinguishing at-risk MASH from simple steatosis matters clinically: in a prospective cohort of 413 patients undergoing liver biopsy and magnetic resonance elastography, a simplified at-risk definition captured a substantially broader group of pharmacotherapy candidates than the stricter NAFLD Activity Score-based definition (122 vs. 77 patients), and optimized liver-stiffness cutoffs on MRE (2.8–6.4 kPa) improved sensitivity for at-risk MASH from 50% to 80% relative to AASLD-recommended thresholds [@Li2026Simplified]. Getting this stratification right is central to treatment selection, since resmetirom and semaglutide — the first agents to receive accelerated approval specifically for MASH — are indicated on the basis of this at-risk designation [@Chan2026Pharmacological; @Li2026Simplified]. At the far end of the disease spectrum, compensated MASH-related cirrhosis remains a distinct and largely unmet therapeutic problem: concurrent metabolic dysfunction, persistent inflammation, stabilized fibrosis, and portal hypertension make this population substantially harder to treat than non-cirrhotic MASH, and although GLP-1/glucagon receptor dual agonists and fibroblast growth factor 21 analogues have advanced into trials for this stage, most candidates tested so far have not demonstrated clear histological or clinical benefit [@Zeng2026Drug].

The pathophysiological rationale for incretin-based therapy in MASLD rests on the tight mechanistic coupling between insulin resistance, glucagon dysregulation, and hepatic lipid handling. Hepatic steatosis develops when insulin resistance drives increased adipose tissue lipolysis and de novo lipogenesis, overwhelming the liver's capacity for fatty-acid oxidation and export, while chronic low-grade inflammation, oxidative stress, and gut microbiota alterations promote the transition from steatosis to lipotoxic injury, inflammation, and fibrogenesis [@Chianetta2026Emerging]. Glucagon itself is increasingly recognized as more than a counter-regulatory hormone to insulin: it regulates energy balance and hepatic lipid metabolism, and glucagon receptor antagonism — despite potent glucose-lowering effects — has been abandoned in clinical development because it worsens hepatic steatosis and promotes weight gain, underscoring that glucagon signaling must be modulated rather than simply blocked [@Kitamura2026Role; @Kushner2026Cardiovascular]. This multi-hormonal, multi-organ crosstalk is now conceptualized within the cardiovascular-kidney-liver-metabolic (CKLM), or unified cardiometabolic disease, continuum: MASLD, type 2 diabetes, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease share upstream drivers — visceral adiposity, ceramide-mediated lipotoxicity, NF-κB/NLRP3-driven inflammation, gut-derived endotoxemia, and endothelial dysfunction — such that hepatic, cardiac, and renal disease should be understood as manifestations of a single progressive process rather than independent conditions [@QuirinoVela2026The; @Anagnostopoulou2026Therapies; @Tsai2026Metabolic]. This framing explains why cardiovascular disease, not liver failure, remains the leading cause of death in patients with MASLD [@Amorim2026GLP], and why therapies capable of intervening simultaneously across the CKLM axis are of particular interest. The economic and demographic scale of the problem reinforces the urgency: obesity alone accounted for an estimated 2.2% of global gross domestic product in 2019, a figure projected to exceed 3% by 2060, and its growth is now fastest in rural and low- to middle-income countries as urbanization, sedentary lifestyles, and ultra-processed food consumption spread [@Henney2026The]. Individual susceptibility within this metabolic milieu is not uniform: genetic variation at the PNPLA3 locus (rs738409) and at the GLP-1 receptor gene itself (GLP1R rs761387, rs6923761) has been shown to modulate treatment response, with the GLP1R rs761387 G allele independently predicting a blunted glycemic response to GLP-1RA therapy, pointing toward a future role for pharmacogenomic stratification in MASLD care [@Toffoli2026Comparative].

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) were developed originally as glucose-lowering agents for T2DM, but their pleiotropic actions — appetite suppression, delayed gastric emptying, reduced hepatic lipogenesis and lipotoxicity, improved insulin sensitivity, and attenuation of systemic inflammation — have positioned them as disease-modifying therapies across the CKLM continuum [@Zhou2026From; @Amorim2026GLP]. Liraglutide, an early GLP-1RA, demonstrated proof-of-concept efficacy in the LEAN trial, achieving steatohepatitis resolution without fibrosis worsening in 39% of patients versus 9% with placebo, while semaglutide has shown dose-dependent histologic resolution rates up to 59% in phase 2 testing and, in an interim phase 3 analysis in F2–F3 MASH, resolution without fibrosis worsening in 62.9% of patients versus 34.3% on placebo [@Amorim2026GLP]. Beyond mono-agonism, the field has moved toward dual and triple incretin-based agonists that co-activate the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor and, in some cases, the glucagon receptor alongside the GLP-1 receptor. Tirzepatide, a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist, achieved MASH resolution in 44–62% of patients in the SYNERGY-NASH trial (versus 10% with placebo), with concomitant fibrosis improvement in up to 51% [@Amorim2026GLP], and has demonstrated broader metabolic benefit across pancreatic, adipose, hepatic, cardiovascular, renal, and central nervous system targets in the SURPASS and SURMOUNT trial programs [@Khan2026Tirzepatide]. Triple agonists and GLP-1/glucagon receptor dual agonists such as survodutide, mazdutide, pemvidutide, retatrutide, and cotadutide are similarly under active clinical investigation, with a pooled analysis of six randomized trials (961 participants) showing that these polyagonists significantly increase MASH resolution or histological improvement without fibrosis worsening (RR 3.32, 95% CI 2.28–4.84) and fibrosis improvement without MASH worsening (RR 1.49, 95% CI 1.15–1.94) relative to placebo [@Santos2026Efficacy]. Cardiovascular outcome trials for GLP-1 monoagonists — LEADER (liraglutide), SUSTAIN-6 and SELECT (semaglutide), and REWIND (dulaglutide) — have independently established reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events, reinforcing the liver-heart axis rationale for this drug class in MASLD [@Amorim2026GLP].

Until the recent approvals of resmetirom and semaglutide, no pharmacotherapy had been specifically approved for MASLD or MASH, leaving lifestyle modification as the sole foundational intervention despite its well-documented difficulty to sustain [@Chan2026Pharmacological]. This absence of approved options, combined with the rapid expansion of incretin-based agents originally developed for T2DM and obesity, has created both an opportunity and a synthesis challenge: evidence spans mechanistic studies, placebo-controlled histologic trials, real-world comparative-effectiveness analyses against sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors and other agents, and emerging data in the cardiovascular-kidney-liver-metabolic population, but findings vary considerably by drug, disease stage, comparator, and outcome definition.

Existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses of incretin-based therapy in MASLD, however, remain fragmented along drug-class and outcome-domain lines. Several are restricted to a single mono-agonist — semaglutide specifically [@Khan2026Therapeutic; @Peng2026Clinical] or GLP-1RAs as an undifferentiated class, without separating evidence for newer dual/triple agonists [@Mahoon2026Therapeutic; @Wu2026Efficacy; @Hu2026Glucagonlike] — while the syntheses that do incorporate dual and triple agonists [@Santos2026Efficacy] or construct network meta-analyses spanning SGLT2 inhibitors and combination regimens [@Tang2026Updating] typically pool evidence from multiple proprietary databases (MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL) supplemented by grey literature, limiting reproducibility for readers without institutional access, and none directly benchmarks monoagonist against dual/triple-agonist evidence within a single PRISMA-compliant framework focused specifically on MASLD/MASH liver histologic and imaging endpoints.

This gap motivates the present review: whether the incremental hepatic benefit of dual and triple incretin-based agonism over GLP-1 monotherapy is discernible and generalizable when the evidence base is restricted to a single, freely accessible, transparently reproducible source — PubMed — has not been specifically addressed. This review closes that gap by applying a PRISMA 2020-compliant, PubMed-only search strategy to systematically identify and synthesize evidence comparing GLP-1 receptor monoagonists against dual and triple incretin-based agonists on MASLD/MASH liver-related outcomes, situating these findings within the broader mechanistic, comparative-effectiveness, and safety landscape described above. This review synthesizes the current evidence on GLP-1RA and multi-agonist efficacy, safety, and clinical positioning for MASLD and MASH. Subsequent sections examine the mechanistic basis for incretin-based hepatic protection, review randomized controlled trial and meta-analytic evidence for GLP-1 monoagonists and dual/triple agonists on histologic, biochemical, and imaging endpoints, evaluate real-world and comparative-effectiveness data against SGLT2 inhibitors and other pharmacotherapies, and consider safety, patient selection, and unresolved questions — including durability of benefit, efficacy in compensated cirrhosis, and the role of these agents within the broader CKLM management framework.

This review pursues the following specific objectives:

1. To systematically identify and synthesize randomized controlled trial and observational evidence on GLP-1 receptor monoagonists (e.g., liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide) for MASLD/MASH liver-related outcomes, including histologic resolution, fibrosis stage, and non-invasive imaging and biochemical markers.
2. To synthesize evidence on dual and triple incretin-based agonists (GIP/GLP-1 co-agonists, GLP-1/glucagon receptor dual agonists, and triple agonists) for the same liver-related outcomes, and to compare the magnitude and consistency of benefit against GLP-1 monotherapy.
3. To characterize the mechanistic basis for incretin-based hepatoprotection and its relationship to the broader cardiovascular-kidney-liver-metabolic (CKLM) disease continuum.
4. To evaluate real-world and comparative-effectiveness evidence for GLP-1RAs and multi-agonists relative to SGLT2 inhibitors and other pharmacotherapies in MASLD/MASH.
5. To characterize the safety profile, tolerability, and patient-selection considerations for incretin-based therapy across disease stages, including compensated MASH-related cirrhosis.
6. To identify unresolved questions and evidence gaps — including durability of benefit, efficacy in cirrhosis, and the potential role of pharmacogenomic stratification — that should guide future research and clinical practice.
